CHIEF COMPLAINT

Upper respiratory infection.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Andrew Campbell is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history of depression, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension. He presents today with an upper respiratory infection.

The onset of his symptoms began 1 week ago when he started working in the yard. He notes that he was doing some landscaping and was carrying heavy bags of soil. He states that he started to feel really tired and was short of breath. He believes that he caught his first cold and it just got worse.

The patient denies coughing up anything. He does report feeling warm, but he thinks this was due to exertion. He also reports experiencing elbow pain and knee pain, which he believes was due to lifting the bags.

In terms of his depression, the patient reports that it has been a crazy year and a half. He notes that he has been doing well with it for the most part. His wife got him into barre classes to help him relax, which she believes is working.

The patient reports that his diet has been good for the most part, except for house parties and things like that. However, he notes that his blood sugar levels have not been elevated since this episode of his diabetes.

In terms of his high blood pressure, the patient reports that he has been monitoring his blood pressure at home regularly while at work. However, on weekends, he does not monitor it as much. The patient confirms that he is taking his medication as prescribed.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Respiratory: Denies coughing up anything. Endorses shortness of breath at rest.
• Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or dyspnea on exertion.
• Neurological: Endorses muscle aches and joint pain.
• Psychiatric: Endorses depression.
• Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea or vomiting or diarrhea.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• Respiratory: Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with scattered ronchi bilaterally; clears with cough.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Chest x-ray obtained today in office review is unremarkable for any evidence of airspace disease or pneumonia.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Upper respiratory infection.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today with an upper respiratory infection. His symptoms began 1 week ago when he started working in the yard and was carrying heavy bags of soil. He denies coughing up anything but endorses shortness of breath at rest. The patient denies fever but endorses feeling warm due to exertion.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I discussed the nature of viral syndrome with the patient today in office and explained that this will resolve in a couple of days without treatment other than over-the-counter medication for symptom relief such as Robitussin for cough and Tylenol or ibuprofen for fever.
- Medical Treatment: We will send a COVID-19 test to rule out COVID-19 exposure today in office.
2. Depression.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient reports being well with depression for the most part but notes it has been a crazy year and half lately due to work stressors at home as well as work-related stressors at work; however, he denies any current depressive symptoms such as changes in appetite or sleep patterns or decreased interest in activities once enjoyed; however, endorses muscle aches and joint pain which may be related to lifting heavy bags while working outdoors recently but also endorses elbow pain bilaterally which may be related to lifting heavy bags while working outdoors recently as well as knee pain bilaterally which may be related to lifting heavy bags while working outdoors recently; however, these symptoms have resolved since yesterday when they were present initially so they are likely related to lifting heavy bags while working outdoors recently rather than depression itself.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I discussed treatment options including medication or psychotherapy if needed today in office with the patient who expressed interest in continuing barre classes as an alternative therapy option for managing stress; however, we discussed starting medical treatment if needed due to ongoing symptoms despite alternative therapy options being effective so far; we also discussed referring him to psychotherapy if needed if medical treatment does not provide relief from symptoms after 3 months so we can reassess at that time if needed.
- Medical Treatment: Continue barre classes as an alternative therapy option for managing stress; refer him to psychotherapy if needed after 3 months if medical treatment does not provide relief from symptoms so we can reassess at that time if needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Annual exam.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Andrea Roberts is a 52-year-old female with a past medical history significant for rheumatoid arthritis, atrial fibrillation, and reflux who presents today for her annual exam. She has been walking like I told her to and exercising and doing yoga, and that has actually helped with her arthritis a lot, just the constant movement. She has not had any joint pain recently.

She is still taking methotrexate once a week without any issues. She denies any issues with that.

She is still having palpitations. The last one she had was about a week ago. She has noticed that when she starts to get stressed, they start to flare up again. She has been trying meditation, trying running with her dog to try and relieve the stress but it has not really been working.

She cut out soda and that seemed to help, and the medication's been helping too. She has not had a flare up in over 5 months.

She endorses nasal congestion due to allergies.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Cardiovascular: Endorses palpitations.
• Respiratory: Endorses nasal congestion due to allergies.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm at this time. Slight 2/6 systolic ejection murmur heard over the heart. No murmurs heard over the lungs.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Event monitor: Positive for conversion pause.
Autoimmune panel: Normal.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Rheumatoid Arthritis.
- Medical Reasoning: Her current methotrexate prescription appears to be effective in controlling her symptoms at this time.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the importance of continuing on methotrexate 2.5 mg once weekly as prescribed.
- Medical Treatment: Continue methotrexate 2.5 mg once weekly as prescribed. If she needs a referral back to see the rheumatologist, let me know but I think everything seems stable now.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with the recommended medical treatment plan.
2. Atrial Fibrillation.
- Medical Reasoning: Her symptoms are consistent with atrial fibrillation with conversion pauses which may be related to stress or anxiety triggers. We discussed that we will refer her to cardiology for cardiac ablation which will map out where that rhythm is coming from and burn it so it does not come back.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the importance of maintaining a normal sinus rhythm at this time given her age and symptoms of atrial fibrillation with conversion pauses which may be related to stress or anxiety triggers.
- Medical Treatment: Refer cardiology for cardiac ablation which will map out where that rhythm is coming from and burn it so it does not come back.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with the recommended medical treatment plan.
3. Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD).
- Medical Reasoning: Her current protonix prescription appears to be effective in controlling her symptoms at this time, however we discussed dietary modifications such as avoiding coffee and spicy foods which have also been helpful in managing her symptoms.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the importance of continuing on protonix 40 mg daily as prescribed along with dietary modifications such as avoiding coffee and spicy foods which have also been helpful in managing her symptoms.
- Medical Treatment: Continue protonix 40 mg daily as prescribed along with dietary modifications such as avoiding coffee and spicy foods which have also been helpful in managing her symptoms if needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Hyperglycemia.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Albert Powell is a 62-year-old male with a past medical history significant for depression, type 2 diabetes, and kidney transplant. He presents to the emergency room for follow-up. The patient was seen in the emergency room over the weekend due to elevated blood sugar. He was not admitted to the hospital. The patient reports that he has been having trouble monitoring his diet due to being busy with work and social activities. He notes that he has been eating fast food on the weekends and grabbing meals at the cafeteria during the week.

The patient reports that his blood sugar was elevated, but he is feeling better now.

The patient reports that he has been taking Lantus insulin as prescribed by his physician.

PAST HISTORY

The patient reports a history of depression.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS

The patient reports taking Lantus insulin.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Denies chest pain or shortness of breath. Denies lightheadedness or dizziness.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
• Cardiovascular: Carotid bruits are absent. Slight 2/6 systolic ejection murmur heard in all fields.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
• Blood glucose: 162 mg/dL.
• Diabetes labs: Hemoglobin A1c is 8.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
• Hyperglycemia.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's elevated blood glucose level is consistent with his history of type 2 diabetes and poor dietary habits.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed dietary modifications with the patient today. I advised him to increase his Lantus insulin dose to 20 units at night and continue monitoring his blood sugar levels.
- Medical Treatment: Increase Lantus insulin dose to 20 units at night.
- Additional Testing: Order hemoglobin A1c in a couple months.
• Depression.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's current symptoms are consistent with depression. He has been doing well with meditation, but we will hold off on medication or therapy at this time.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed current coping mechanisms with the patient today. I advised him to continue meditation for a couple more months before we revisit medical treatment options if needed.
- Medical Treatment: Hold off on medical treatment or therapy at this time, but encourage him to call me if he needs anything.
• Kidney Transplant Status.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's kidney function appears stable on immunosuppression medications as per Dr. Reyes' last visit three weeks ago.

It's been kind of a stressful summer. Kinda adjusting to everything in the fall and so far it's been good, but lack of sleep, it's been really getting to me.

The patient reports that he has tried everything from melatonin to meditation to stretching out every morning when he gets up. Nothing really seems to help though.

In terms of his osteoporosis, he is currently taking Fosamax 1 tab per week. He denies any issues with his joints or any issues like broken bones recently.

The patient last saw the neurologist 6 months ago and is taking the medication as prescribed. He denies any additional weakness, including his right leg which was previously noted to have improved.

He endorses insomnia but denies any other issues such as chest pain or shortness of breath.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Neurological: Endorses insomnia.
• Musculoskeletal: Denies joint pain or stiffness.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Lawrence Walker is a 62-year-old male with a past medical history significant for type 1 diabetes, congestive heart failure, depression, and reflux. He presents with complaints of shortness of breath. The onset of his symptoms began approximately 10 days ago. He notes that he has noticed swelling in his legs. He denies chest pain, fever, chills, cough, or belly pain.

Mr. Walker reports that he has been going to house parties and eating salty foods which he believes may be contributing to his current symptoms. He also reports feeling lethargic.

Regarding his diabetes, he states that he has been doing well with his insulin pump and has not noticed any spikes in his blood sugar levels recently. However, he admits to consuming chocolate bars regularly.

In terms of his depression, Mr. Walker states that it has been a challenging year and a half for him. He reports trying natural solutions such as stretching outdoors every morning but notes that the weather change has made this difficult for him at this time. He denies suicidal ideation.

Regarding his reflux, Mr. Walker reports that he was previously prescribed omeprazole 20 mg daily and was advised to cut back on red Bull and caffeine consumption as well as limit alcohol intake during the holiday season.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Respiratory: Endorses shortness of breath.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
• Neck: No jugular venous distension or carotid bruits.
• Cardiovascular: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur.
• Respiratory: Crackles bilaterally at the bases.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
• Chest X-ray: No evidence of airspace disease.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Acute heart failure exacerbation.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents with shortness of breath which began approximately 10 days ago. His physical exam reveals bilateral crackles at the bases consistent with pulmonary edema and 1+ pitting edema bilaterally consistent with fluid overload.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I have discussed the nature of his condition with him today in detail and have advised him to follow up with me if his weight is not going down or if it is going up or if he gets more short of breath at rest.
- Medical Treatment: We will start him on Lasix 40 mg daily to help reduce fluid overload. I want him to weigh himself every day.
- Additional Testing: Chest x-ray was reviewed today in office which showed no evidence of airspace disease but does not rule out fluid overload.
2. Type 1 diabetes.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today for a routine checkup for type 1 diabetes management but notes that he has been doing well lately without any spikes in blood sugar levels recently however admits to consuming chocolate bars regularly.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I have discussed the importance of monitoring blood sugar levels regularly with him today in detail and advised him to follow up with his endocrinologist soon for further evaluation and management recommendations including ordering a hemoglobin A1c within the next month or so as well as scheduling a recent eye exam.
3. Depression.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today for an evaluation for depression which began approximately 1 year ago due to stress from work related issues however notes that it has been challenging lately due to other stressors such as holiday season stressors however denies suicidal ideation at this time.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I have discussed the nature of his condition with him today in detail and advised him against taking any medications at this time but referred him to psychiatry for talk therapy to help manage symptoms.

Left shoulder and elbow pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Mr. James is a 64-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of left shoulder and elbow pain. He reports that he has been experiencing constant pain in his left shoulder and left elbow for approximately 5 months, since he fell 5 months ago while going up stairs. He states that he was walking up a flight of stairs to his house when his feet slipped on ice, and he fell on his left side. He believes that his left shoulder and wrist took the brunt of the fall. The pain has been present since then.

The patient reports that his pain is worse when he lifts weights, but he has been trying to keep up with his routine of 2 days per week. He notes that he has not been able to lift more than 15 or 20 pounds due to the pain. He also reports that he has stopped hitting the gym over the past 1-2 weeks because the pain was not worth it.

The patient denies any numbness or tingling in his left arm or hand at any point.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports left shoulder and elbow pain.
Neurological: Denies numbness or tingling.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

General Examination: Normal vital signs. Denies fever, chills, or weight loss.
Musculoskeletal Examination: Left shoulder and elbow tender to palpation over sa space bilaterally without warmth, erythema, or deformity. Positive Hawkins-Kennedy test and Neer's test bilaterally. Normal proximal and distal upper extremity strength intact median radial ulnar sensation to L5 dermatome intact abduction to 90 degrees bilaterally.
note.assessment_and_plan:

Impingement syndrome of the left shoulder.
Plan discussed with patient in detail today.
Referral requested for Dr. Martha Rivera for physical therapy 2 days per week.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Acne.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Kayla Ward is a 15-year-old female who presents for a new visit with her mother for acne located on the face, which started about 2 years ago and is present most every day. She has been using Persa-Gel and washing regularly, which is somewhat helpful. There are no associated symptoms including itching, bleeding, or pain.

The patient denies any flare-ups with her periods. She reports that she gets a regular period and has been getting one for approximately 2 years. Her biggest flare was when she started school sports in the fall due to all the sweating.

The patient notes that she has been doing a good job with her facial care regimen but it does not seem to help as much as they wanted.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Skin: Denies itching, bleeding, or pain.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

General Examination: The patient appears well-developed and well-nourished for her age. Her vital signs are within normal limits. No fever or distress.
Skin: Multiple benign nevi on the trunk and extremities. Scattered skin-colored papules. Open and closed comedones. Erythematous papules on the face, primarily on the forehead and central cheeks and chin.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Mild to moderate acne.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents with mild to moderate acne, mostly comedonal with small inflammatory component.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the nature of her acne in detail today. I advised her that we will start with a topical therapy first. Every morning, she will wash her face with a mild cleanser then use a moisturizer labeled “noncomedogenic,” with SPF 30 or higher. This means it won’t clog your pores. Now, in the evening, wash her face with the same cleanser and allow it to dry. Apply adapalene 0.1% cream in a thin layer to the areas where she generally gets acne.
- Medical Treatment: We will start off using this a few nights a week and slowly work up to using it every night if needed due to cost or insurance coverage issues at this point we can try different gel over-the-counter if needed followed by Clean & Clear Persa-Gel in a thin layer or where she generally gets acne then noncomedogenic moisturizer.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with the recommended medical treatment plan.
- Additional Testing/Procedures: We will follow up in 6 months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Hematuria.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Mrs. Kelly Wood is a 41-year-old female who presents for renal ultrasound due to hematuria. The patient reports that she has had bright red urine for the past 6 weeks, and she was constantly having to urinate and it hurt terribly. She denies flank pain or lower back tenderness at this time. She notes that she passed 2 small stones last week after scheduling this appointment.

The patient reports that her symptoms have improved since passing the stones.

SOCIAL HISTORY

The patient reports that she drinks more Mountain Dew than water.

MEDICAL HISTORY

The patient reports a history of chronic urolithiasis.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Denies weight loss, fevers, chills, or malaise.
• Genitourinary: Reports hematuria.
• Musculoskeletal: Denies flank pain or lower back tenderness.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
• Abdomen: No flank pain. Anti-Guerrero exam is normal.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
• Urine dipstick: Color yellow, appearance clear, leukocytes negative, nitrate negative, urobilinogen 0.2 EU/dL, protein negative, pH 5.5, blood trace, intact, specific gravity 1.020, ketone negative, bilirubin negative, glucose negative.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
• Primary diagnosis: Hematuria.
• Secondary diagnosis: Chronic urolithiasis.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient's renal ultrasound revealed a left renal stone non-obstructing at 6 mm in size. The patient has had bright red urine for the past 6 weeks and was constantly having to urinate and it hurt terribly. She denies flank pain or lower back tenderness at this time. She notes that she passed 2 small stones last week after scheduling this appointment.
• Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the formation of kidney stones can not be attributed to a particular cause but several factors increase the risk such as dehydration family history certain foods digestive tract disease and certain medical conditions. We discussed dietary recommendations such as drinking half of her body weight in ounces of water per day and avoiding sugary drinks like Mountain Dew. We also discussed food to avoid such as salty processed food because they are high in sodium and reduce the amount of beef poultry fish and pork. The patient should avoid foods rich in sodium oxalate such as spinach chocolate beets rhubarb and soy products.
• Medical Treatment: No surgical intervention is recommended at this time due to the non-obstructive nature of the left renal stone.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Status post mitral valve repair.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Melissa Sanchez is a 58-year-old female who presents for a follow-up status post mitral valve repair. She was seen in office on 9/17/2020, at which time we felt that she was doing quite well from a cardiac standpoint, and so we recommended she continue with the same medication. ECG taken on 12/26/2020 reveals atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular response. T-wave inversion anteriorly. Compared to the previous study, there are no significant changes.

The patient reports that she is feeling better overall. She was having a rough time before surgery, but she thinks she is overall pretty good now though. She denies any new symptoms at this time. She does report that she is still getting some chest pains sometimes and her breathing gets shallow. However, she has learned what she can and cannot do and if she feels like that when exerting herself, she slows down a bit which helps and then when she goes back to it later, she can usually finish whatever it was doing.

She estimates that these episodes last only a few minutes and then they disappear for a couple of weeks. When they happen, she just takes the day nice and slow and does not push herself. She estimates that these episodes occur often enough for her to notice.

The patient reports that she has been trying to keep up with her medications regularly. There are a lot of extra pills now but she has a reminder app so she does pretty well.

She denies any side effects from the medications at all except for the atenolol which makes her irritable in the beginning but it doesn’t seem to bother her as much now.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Respiratory: Denies dyspnea on exertion.
• Cardiovascular: Reports chest pain.
• Neurological: Denies confusion or altered mental status.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• Head and Neck: No JVD detected in neck examination.
• Respiratory: Reduced breath sounds bilaterally without wheezes or rales; Auscultation of Lungs clear to auscultation; No wheezes or rales heard bilaterally.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
ECG taken on 12/26/2020 reveals atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response. T-wave inversion anteriorly compared to previous study there are no significant changes.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Melissa Sanchez is a 58-year-old female who presents for a follow-up status post mitral valve repair.
ECG taken on 12/26/2020 reveals atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response. T-wave inversion anteriorly compared to previous study there are no significant changes.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient’s ECG today shows atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response as well as t-wave inversion anteriorly compared to previous studies there are no significant changes.
• Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed lifestyle modifications such as regular exercise which will help control symptoms of atrial fibrillation as well as medication adherence with Coumadin 4 mg daily Lasix 40 mg daily Atenolol 50 mg daily.
• Medical Treatment: Continue Coumadin 4 mg daily Lasix 40 mg daily Atenolol 50 mg daily.

Ongoing management of psoriatic arthritis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Judy Gomez is a 61-year-old female who presents for ongoing management of psoriatic arthritis. She reports that her pain has been well-controlled on methotrexate. She was previously taking prednisone 1 mg daily, but she has been able to discontinue this due to her improvement in symptoms. She notes that she will occasionally take an extra dose of prednisone when she has a day off and is moving around a lot, but this is not frequent. The patient denies any issues with her methotrexate, stating that she took it once after getting her COVID-19 vaccine and experienced worsening symptoms, but after taking it again the following week, her symptoms improved.

The patient reports bruising with minimal pain when she bumps herself. She denies any history of bleeding disorders or taking medications that could cause bruising.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports joint pain in the feet and knees.
Skin: Denies any skin lesions or rashes.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Skin: Examination of the extremities reveals ridging in the nails consistent with psoriasis.

She notes that she will occasionally take an extra dose of prednisone when she has a day off and is moving around a lot, but this is not frequent.

The patient denies any issues with her methotrexate, stating that she took it once after getting her COVID-19 vaccine and experienced worsening symptoms, but after taking it again the following week, her symptoms improved.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Newly diagnosed allergic asthma.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Charles Sullivan is a 45-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of new onset shortness of breath. The onset of his symptoms began approximately 2 years ago when he moved into a large plot of land in the country. He enjoys hunting and has a refrigerator full of venison at home. He notes that he has noticed that his breathing is not what it used to be, and he considers himself to be pretty healthy. He states that he catches his breath more than he used to and that he is short of breath. He denies any other symptoms with his breathing, but notes that his eyes water when he gets eyebugers from his dog.

The patient reports that the last time this occurred, he went to the urgent care and they gave him a nebulizer that helped. He was prescribed an inhaler which he uses now when he feels the symptoms coming on. He denies any rash with this, but does report some nausea and vomiting when heavy drinking.

The patient also reports that he experiences diarrhea once after heavy drinking.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Respiratory: Denies coughing, wheezing, or dyspnea on exertion.
• Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or palpitations.
• Gastrointestinal: Reports diarrhea after heavy drinking.
• Skin: Denies rash.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Respiratory: Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with mild expiratory wheezing.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Chest x-ray obtained today was normal in appearance.
Pulmonary function test obtained today was normal in appearance.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Newly diagnosed allergic asthma.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient's history and physical examination findings are consistent with newly diagnosed allergic asthma. His pulmonary function test and chest x-ray were both normal in appearance, which makes an infectious etiology less likely. His history of eyebugers from his dog is also consistent with allergic asthma.
• Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the nature of his diagnosis in detail today. I have also provided him with information regarding Singulair 10 mg once daily as well as allergy testing options including skin testing and immunotherapy if necessary.
• Medical Treatment: Continue albuterol inhaler as prescribed by urgent care provider for symptom management until we can identify triggers through allergy testing. Prescribed Singulair 10 mg once daily for long-term management of asthma.
• Additional Testing: Schedule skin testing for next week.

Low back pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Bryan Brooks is a 39-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of low back pain. The onset of his pain began 2 hours ago when he was raking leaves in his yard. He denies any prior history of similar episodes. He notes that he has had an episode of low back pain 3 years ago, which resolved after a day.

The patient reports that he has been doing minimal physical activity lately and that his partner has been doing all the yard work. He denies any history of trauma or injury.

The patient describes his pain as radiating down to his right foot, with some improvement with sitting and worsening with standing. He notes that icing and Advil have not provided relief. He also notes that a hot shower has provided some relief.

PAST HISTORY

The patient reports that he had an episode of low back pain 3 years ago, which resolved after a day.

SOCIAL HISTORY

The patient reports that he is married and notes that his partner is also experiencing pain when he stands up.

1. Low back strain.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's symptoms are consistent with low back strain, likely secondary to overuse or repetitive strain from yard work.

- Medical Treatment: We have prescribed meloxicam for pain management and physical therapy to improve strength and flexibility.
- Additional Testing: We will follow up in 2 weeks if her symptoms do not improve.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Non-healing right foot ulcer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Mr. Hernandez is a 40-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of a non-healing right foot ulcer. The patient reports that he has had the ulcer for approximately 2 months and it has recently become red and is draining. He denies any trauma to his foot when he got it, but believes that he may have gotten it from walking barefoot on the beach.

The patient states that he did see his primary care physician before coming in today, and they prescribed him medication for his ulcer. However, he has not yet picked up the medication from the pharmacy.

The patient reports that his ulcer sometimes throbs, but he does not have specific pain. He notes that his biggest concern is that it started to drain and it looks a little red. He has not had this before.

Regarding his diabetes, the patient states that he takes his medication but does not check his sugar levels regularly. He estimates that his last A1C was around 10.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Skin: Reports redness, drainage, edema, and increased pressure around the ulcer site.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• General Examination: Vital signs are within normal limits. No fever present.
• Neurological Examination: Normal sensation in all extremities.
• Musculoskeletal Examination: Examination of right foot reveals a 1 x 2 cm circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot proximal to the 5th MTP joint. There is some redness and drainage present. There is edema around it with fluid leaking out of it. No necrosis or odor present. No bony exposure.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of right foot taken today reveals no evidence of osteomyelitis.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Mr. Hernandez is a 40-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of a non-healing right foot ulcer.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient's current symptoms are consistent with an infected diabetic foot ulcer.
• Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed treatment options with the patient today including performing an ABI ankle brachial index to determine blood supply in his foot, performing debridement to remove dead tissue, prescribing clindamycin for 7 days to treat infection, and obtaining a surgical shoe for protection while healing.
• Medical Treatment: An ABI ankle brachial index will be ordered today to determine blood supply in his foot. Debridement will be performed today to remove dead tissue from the wound site. Clindamycin will be prescribed for 7 days at 400 mg twice daily to treat infection. A surgical shoe will be obtained for him to wear while healing.
• Additional Testing: An ABI ankle brachial index will be ordered today.
• Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with recommended medical treatment plan.

The patient denies any specific injury.

The patient reports that he is currently not seeing a podiatrist due to his PCP referring him to us today.

Musculoskeletal: Reports stability issues with his feet.
Neurological: Reports neuropathy.
note.objective_exam:

• Temperature: 98.1°F.
• Heart rate: 72 bpm.
• Respirations: 16 breaths per minute.
• Blood pressure: 110/65 mmHg.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
• Right foot x-ray shows no evidence of osteomyelitis.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
• Diabetic Foot Ulcer.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents with a non-healing wound on his right foot. His last hemoglobin A1C was elevated at 8%. We reviewed his x-ray and there is no evidence of osteomyelitis present. We also reviewed his ankle brachial index (ABI) prior to today’s visit and it will be ordered again today as we will be performing debridement in office and prescribing collagenase ointment for application once daily and covering with dry sterile dressing until we see improvement in wound healing. If ABI indicates poor blood supply, we may refer him to vascular specialist.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the importance of getting his diabetes under control in order to heal this wound effectively. We also discussed ways he can modify his diet without overdoing it in order to bring down his hemoglobin A1c level into a little better range.
- Medical Treatment: Debridement will be performed in office today and collagenase ointment prescribed for application once daily until we see improvement in wound healing. Surgical shoe prescribed for pressure off area until further notice.
- Additional Testing Ordered: Ankle brachial index (ABI) ordered today.

Right knee pain.

Mr. William Russell is a 57-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right knee pain. The onset of his pain began 1 week ago when he sustained an injury at a trampoline park. He states that he heard a pop and instant pain when he was on the trampoline. He denies any previous history of knee injuries.

The patient reports that he has not been consistent with his exercise regimen and only engages in recreational activities such as trampolining. He denies any regular exercise regimen.

The patient reports that his pain is primarily located on the lateral aspect of his right knee. He states that he has not taken any medication for his pain, but has been taking Tylenol as needed. The patient reports that the Tylenol has not provided relief for his pain.

The patient denies icing or using heat for his pain, but does elevate his leg when it hurts.

PAST HISTORY

Mr. Russell reports that he has hypertension and type 2 diabetes.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Mr. Russell reports that he does not regularly exercise and only engages in recreational activities such as trampolining.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs.
• Respiratory: Clear bilaterally to auscultation.
• Musculoskeletal: Examination of the right knee reveals ecchymosis and edema along the lateral aspect of the knee, but no effusion. Range of motion is intact, but there is a slight limp present.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of the right knee revealed no evidence of fracture or bony abnormality.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Right knee pain.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient sustained an injury at a trampoline park which resulted in lateral ligament strain.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed conservative treatment options including physical therapy to strengthen the muscles around the area and prevent further injury if necessary.
- Medical Treatment: I have prescribed meloxicam 15 mg daily for pain and swelling. I have also referred him to physical therapy to help strengthen the muscles around the area and prevent further injury if necessary.
- Additional Testing: X-ray was ordered to rule out fracture or bony abnormality.
2. Hypertension.
- Medical Reasoning: His blood pressure is elevated at this visit, which may be due to non-adherence with medication or other factors such as diet or lifestyle changes.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed lifestyle modifications including diet, exercise, and stress reduction techniques to help manage blood pressure.
- Medical Treatment: Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily as prescribed by another provider; order echocardiogram due to elevated blood pressure; we will discuss medication modification if necessary after reviewing results from echocardiogram.
3. Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Medical Reasoning: His blood sugar levels appear to be improving, however we need more information on long-term control with A1C testing ordered today; lipid panel will also be ordered due to current medication regimen.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Headaches.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Julie Jenkins is a 33-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of headaches. The onset of her headaches began in her teenage years, initially during menses, but has since become more frequent and severe. She notes that her headaches are worse with physical activity. She has noticed that she can get headaches when she is stressed. The patient reports that she has been trying to exercise more in order to lose weight, but she cannot exercise for very long because her headaches return and are worse.

The patient also reports experiencing ringing in her ears for a few months now, and she has started to notice some blurred vision. The vision changes are intermittent and seem to be on the side of her vision. She denies any numbness or tingling in her hands or feet or face.

SOCIAL HISTORY

The patient enjoys running and wears New Balance or Asics shoes.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

VITALS
- Blood pressure: within normal limits.

NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION
- Cranial nerves 1 through 12 are intact including a normal cranial reflex.
- Neurological examination of the face: No facial weakness or numbness.
- Neurological examination of the motor system: Normal gait.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

MRI of the brain was ordered today due to the patient's symptoms. We will follow up with this after it is completed.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's symptoms are concerning for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). Her symptoms include worsening headaches with activity, tinnitus, and changes in vision. These symptoms are consistent with IIH.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the nature of IIH, its treatment options, and lifestyle modifications that can help alleviate symptoms.
- Medical Treatment: We will order an MRI of the brain to confirm our suspicion of IIH. If this confirms our suspicion, we will start treatment with medications such as acetazolamide to decrease intracranial pressure. We will also refer her to a neuro-ophthalmologist for a complete eye exam.
- Additional Testing: An MRI of the brain was ordered today due to the patient's symptoms.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Neck pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

The patient is a 40-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of neck pain. He reports that he was in a car accident 1 week ago, where he hit his back and his neck went forward and his head went forward quickly. He has been experiencing neck pain ever since. The pain is rated 7/10 in severity. The pain is not constant but worsens with movement of the neck. He denies any improvement with ibuprofen, which he has been taking for 5/10 relief.

The patient reports that he is able to turn his head from side to side, but there is pain with this movement. He denies any headaches or visual disturbances. The pain is localized to the back of his neck and radiates into his upper back and shoulder, but denies any pain in these areas.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports left-sided neck pain.
Neurological: Denies headaches, visual disturbances.
Psychiatric: Denies depression or anxiety.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neck Examination: Positive to palpation of the soft tissues of the left side of the neck. Positive pain with flexion and extension of the left cervical spine. Positive pain with lateral bending of the left cervical spine.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
X-ray of cervical spine obtained today, not yet reviewed.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

The patient is a 40-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of neck pain.

After reviewing the patient's history and examination today, I believe that he has developed left-sided neck strain due to a car accident 1 week ago.
Conservative treatment will be initiated today. The patient will be prescribed Motrin 600 mg every 6-8 hours as needed for anti-inflammatory effects. Flexeril 10 mg will be prescribed every 12 hours as needed for muscle relaxation.
I have also ordered an MRI due to concerns about possible concussion or nerve impingement.
I have referred him to either physical rehabilitation or chiropractic care once we receive the results of his MRI for further evaluation and treatment.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Left shoulder pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Bobby Flores is a 56-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of left shoulder pain. The onset of his symptoms began 2 weeks ago when he was doing yard work. He notes that he has been sore all over, but his right shoulder has been particularly sore. He denies any numbness in his arm or hands.

The patient reports that he has had some right shoulder pain in the past due to playing baseball when he was younger. He notes that this is not the same as his current symptoms, which are more on the outside of his right shoulder and tender to palpation. He denies any restriction of motion with his right arm, but does report some pain with movement. His symptoms are worse with activity and improve with rest.

The patient reports that he has been taking Advil and icing as much as possible for pain relief. This has provided some relief, but he still feels sore to the touch.

PAST HISTORY

The patient reports a history of right shoulder pain when he was younger while playing baseball.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neck: No tenderness to palpation at the sternoclavicular or acromioclavicular joints.
Right Shoulder: Limited active and passive range of motion. There is tenderness at the great tuberosity of the humerus. No tenderness at the acromioclavicular joint.
Neurovascular: Capillary refill is less than 3 seconds bilaterally. Sensation to light touch is intact bilaterally.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

3 views of the right shoulder were obtained today and reviewed in office today. There is no fracture.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Left Shoulder Pain.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's symptoms are most likely due to rotator cuff tendinopathy.
- Additional Testing: We will order an MRI for further evaluation.
- Medical Treatment: Continue Tylenol as prescribed by your wife for pain relief. Refer him to physical therapy for 6-8 weeks, starting immediately. If symptoms do not improve, we will consider a steroid injection of his shoulder.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed treatment options in detail today.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Right elbow pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Mark Jackson is a 45-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right elbow pain. The onset of his symptoms began 3 weeks ago when he started playing tennis again. He notes that his pain is located on the outside of his elbow and is worse with activity and better with rest. He denies any trauma to the area. The patient reports that he has tried taking Tylenol and ibuprofen, but they do not provide any relief. He also notes that icing his elbow has not helped with his pain.

The patient reports that he has a history of type 2 diabetes, mild intermittent asthma, and cholecystectomy 10 years ago by Dr. Nelson. He also reports an allergy to penicillin.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right elbow pain.
Cardiovascular: Denies fever.
Respiratory: Reports mild intermittent asthma.
Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain.
Neurological: Denies headaches or dizziness.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

CV: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border unchanged from prior exam.
MSK: Examination of the right elbow reveals moderate lateral epicondylar tenderness. Passive range of motion is limited due to pain. Mild pain with resisted extension of the right wrist.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of the right elbow today shows no acute fracture or other bony abnormality. There is no malalignment or sign of joint effusion.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Acute lateral epicondylitis of the right elbow.
- Medical Reasoning: This is due to overuse likely from increased tennis activity which normally would be good but maybe we are overdoing it a little bit.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I discussed treatment options with the patient today including rest, ice, bracing, and medication for pain control.
- Medical Treatment: I have prescribed a brace for his right forearm which should help with discomfort. I have also prescribed Ultram 50 mg once per day which should help with pain control.
- Additional Testing: We will reevaluate in 4 weeks and if needed possibly order additional imaging or refer him to physical therapy.
2. Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Medical Reasoning: His blood sugar levels are elevated at this time which may be related to recent Easter candy consumption and increased activity level at tennis.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I discussed dietary modifications with him today including limiting carbohydrate intake and increasing fiber intake as well as increasing physical activity level but avoiding repetitive stress on his right arm while doing so.
- Medical Treatment: We will increase metformin to 1000 mg twice per day starting immediately today. I have also ordered a hemoglobin A1c level, CBC blood test, and chem-12 blood test for further evaluation today.
3. Mild acute intermittent asthma.
- Medical Reasoning: His asthma appears to be well controlled at this time on Flovent twice daily and albuterol as needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Asthma.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Betty Lewis is a 66-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of asthma. She reports that she has been experiencing symptoms of asthma for the past 6 months. She states that she has been coughing and wheezing almost every day. She notes that she usually wakes up 2-3 times per night due to her symptoms and will use her albuterol inhaler as needed. She denies any improvement in her symptoms despite using her inhaler as needed.

She reports that her symptoms seem to worsen when she gets sick, but notes that she had a flare-up after visiting her aunt's house due to exposure to her cat. She tries to avoid going there and has not had an issue since.

She states that she has been to urgent care and emergency department on multiple occasions for exacerbations of asthma. She notes that these episodes have required antibiotics, steroids, and prednisone taper packs. Her last exacerbation was approximately 1 month ago.

The patient denies any history of seasonal allergies. She does enjoy going outside and walking, but notes that she is careful due to her coughing and wheezing.

PAST HISTORY

History of asthma.
No history of seasonal allergies.
No history of smoking or tobacco use.
No history of vaping or e-cigarette use.
note.objective_exam:

• Respiratory: Diminished lung sounds throughout with occasional slight expiratory wheeze bilaterally.

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Moderate intermittent asthma.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient's pulmonary function test results are consistent with moderate intermittent asthma.
• Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the importance of consistent use of inhaled steroid inhaler, which will help reduce daily symptoms and need for rescue inhaler use. We also discussed the importance of waiting after using albuterol inhaler before taking additional doses if needed.
• Medical Treatment: I have prescribed Flovent 100 mcg one puff twice per day for inhaled steroid inhaler use. The patient can continue using Ventolin inhaler as needed for rescue inhaler use (2 puffs every 4-6 hours p.r.n.).
• Additional Testing: Pulmonary function test results were reviewed today, which are consistent with moderate intermittent asthma.
• Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with the recommended medical treatment plan.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Chronic lumbar back pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Mr. Larry Garcia is a 41-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of chronic lumbar back pain. The onset of his pain began approximately 2 years ago when he was moving furniture. He describes his pain as sharp stabbing in nature, radiating down to his right leg and even down to his right toe. He also reports difficulty getting comfortable, which is worse when he sits down. He denies any numbness or tingling in the genital or rectal area, as well as weakness. He denies any loss of control of his bladder or bowels.

The patient has tried various treatments including physical therapy and strong pain medications, which were only temporary in nature. He has also been mentioned for surgery in the past but would like to avoid this option.

The patient reports that he is trying to be as active as possible but due to his back pain, he has gained weight over the past few years. He used to enjoy playing golf but this has set him back from doing so.

PAST HISTORY

• Chronic lumbar back pain.
• Quit smoking 20 years ago.
• Denies any family history of spine conditions.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Musculoskeletal: There is no erythema or ecchymosis overlying the skin. Midline tenderness at L4-L5 disk space with right-sided lumbar paravertebral tenderness. Supine straight leg raise test is positive.
Neurological: Decreased sensation to light touch at L4 dermatome on the right lateral thigh.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

MRI of the lumbar spine reveals disc herniation with nerve impingement.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Mr. Larry Garcia is a 41-year-old male who presents today for the evaluation of chronic lumbar back pain.
After reviewing his history and examination findings today, I have had a lengthy discussion with him regarding his symptoms and treatment options available for him today.
Based on his symptoms, examination findings, and review of MRI results, I have diagnosed him with an L4-L5 herniated disk with radiculopathy.
I have recommended that we proceed with a spinal injection with a corticosteroid under fluoroscopy at this time. This should help reduce inflammation causing his pain. We will monitor him and see how he responds to the injection and repeat as necessary up to 4 times per year if needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Right knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Kenneth King is a 44-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right knee pain. The onset of his symptoms began 5 days ago when he was skiing on Lake Martin. He sustained a twisting injury when he landed from a jump and felt like something stretched and then swelled up afterwards. He denies hearing anything pop or feeling anything pop at the time of the injury. He was able to get out of the water by himself but notes that climbing up and squatting or bending is very sore. He has never injured this knee before.

The patient reports that he has been taking Aleve twice a day and applying a cold pack to his knee, which has helped somewhat but he still notes that it is still pretty sore.

PAST HISTORY

The patient reports that he had his tonsils out.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS

The patient reports that he is currently taking Lisinopril 20 mg once daily.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right knee pain, swelling, and ecchymosis. Denies numbness or tingling in his foot.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neck: No lymphadenopathy.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs.
Respiratory: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the right knee reveals ecchymosis, edema, effusion, and decreased range of motion. There is pain with palpation of the right medial knee joint. Negative varus and valgus testing, negative Lachman sign, palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulse.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of the right knee will be ordered.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Right medial collateral ligament strain.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient sustained a twisting injury when he landed from a jump while skiing on Lake Martin 5 days ago. He denies hearing anything pop or feeling anything pop at the time of the injury. He was able to get out of the water by himself but notes that climbing up and squatting or bending is very sore. He has never injured this knee before.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed treatment options with him today including physical therapy to strengthen those muscles around his knee as well as meloxicam 15 mg once daily for pain management.
- Medical Treatment: We will refer him to physical therapy for strengthening exercises around his knee as well as prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once daily for pain management.
2. Hypertension.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient reports that he has been taking Lisinopril 20 mg once daily for hypertension control with blood pressure readings ranging from 120/77 mmHg at home most days.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed treatment options with him today including continuing Lisinopril 20 mg once daily as well as ordering an lipid panel for further evaluation.
- Medical Treatment: Continue Lisinopril 20 mg once daily; order lipid panel.

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
• Incidental finding of right upper lobe lung nodule.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today for the evaluation of an incidental finding of a right upper lobe lung nodule on his CT scan. His symptoms are consistent with bronchitis, but the CT scan revealed a solitary 2 cm nodule in the lateral aspect of the right upper lobe. Given his smoking history, I believe it is likely malignant in nature.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed treatment options in detail today and I have provided him with additional information regarding these options.
- Medical Treatment: I have ordered pulmonary function testing (PFT) to obtain baseline values for his lung function. We will also schedule a PET CT to determine if this nodule is metabolically active or not. If it appears to be metabolically active, we will proceed with surgical removal via video-assisted thoracoscopy (VATS). This procedure will involve making 3 small incisions on the side of his right chest and removing the nodule along with a small portion of his lung under general anesthesia. Post-operatively, we will place a chest tube in place until it is removed bedside on day 2, at which point he will be discharged home on day 3.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with the recommended medical treatment plan.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Difficulty swallowing.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Tyler Green is a 56-year-old male who presents today complaining of difficulty swallowing. He has noticed this over the last 4 to 5 weeks. He describes it as something being stuck in his throat and he has to wash it down on occasion. He denies ever fully choking but admits that he has thought about potentially choking. The patient notes that solids are more likely to get stuck than liquids. He denies any blood in his stools or vomiting blood. He also denies any weight loss or changes in his weight.

The patient reports that he is doing well with his diabetes, taking his metformin as prescribed, and following a healthy diet and exercise plan. His hemoglobin A1c was last checked at 7.4, which was within target range. He denies any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea with the metformin.

PAST HISTORY

The patient reports a history of diabetes and hypertension.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• Neck: No swelling or masses present. Thyroid feels normal without any tenderness or masses.
• Throat: No masses or swelling present. No redness.
• Carotid bruit: Negative.
• Lung exam: Clear bilaterally.
• Heart exam: Normal without murmurs.
• Abdomen: Mild epigastric tenderness without masses or significant swelling present.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Hemoglobin A1c: 7.4
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Tyler Green is a 56-year-old male who presents today complaining of difficulty swallowing.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient's symptoms are consistent with esophageal narrowing, possibly due to a stricture, which can cause dysphagia when eating solids but not liquids.
• Additional Testing/Examination: We will refer him to gastroenterology for an endoscopy and biopsy to evaluate for esophageal narrowing.
• Medical Treatment Plan:
- Continue metformin 500 mg twice daily as prescribed.
- Start Prilosec 20 mg once daily for reflux prevention.
- Advise the patient to chew food frequently when eating solid foods such as steak or meat to prevent them from getting stuck in the esophagus.
- If symptoms worsen, refer him to the emergency department immediately if he experiences difficulty breathing or chest pain.
- Continue Norvasc as prescribed by his primary care physician.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Right ankle pain and instability.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Jerry Cook is a 45-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right ankle pain and instability. The onset of his symptoms began when he was playing basketball with his son, Sean. He reports that he was going for a lap when he landed awkwardly and rolled and twisted his right ankle. He notes that he can see bruising on the outside of his ankle and it is swollen. He has been having trouble walking due to pain and instability in the right ankle. The patient reports that he recently resumed engaging in a consistent gym routine.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right ankle pain and instability.
Skin: Reports right ankle bruising and swelling.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

MSK: Examination of the right ankle reveals exquisite tenderness over the lateral aspect of the distal fibula. There is mild swelling on the lateral side of the ankle with no epidermolysis. Skin is intact. Brisk capillary refill is present without any signs of malalignment. Gait: The patient has difficulty ambulating due to pain in the right ankle.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-rays were obtained today, which are currently being reviewed.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Lateral malleolar fracture.
- Medical Reasoning: The x-ray findings reveal a displaced lateral malleolus at Weber C level, which is consistent with a lateral malleolar fracture. There is no evidence of medial or posterior malleolar fractures.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed treatment options in detail today, including surgery, which will provide stability to the foot while it heals.
- Medical Treatment: We will start him on meloxicam for pain management today.
- Additional Testing: X-rays were obtained today, which are currently being reviewed.
- Surgical Treatment: We will proceed with surgery to place plates and screws to stabilize his foot while it heals.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with the recommended medical treatment plan.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Facial pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Mr. Anthony Miller is a 54-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of facial pain. The onset of his pain began approximately 2 months ago, and it is described as stabbing and shooting in nature. He rates his pain as a 10 out of 10. The pain is localized to the right side of his face, specifically in the right cheek bone area. He notes that the pain is sometimes accompanied by heat, and he has noticed that certain temperatures seem to trigger it. He denies any sensory loss, numbness, or tingling in the right cheek. He denies any right-sided facial weakness. His teeth are symmetric.

The patient reports that he has tried ibuprofen and Motrin without relief. He also tried Tiger Balm without success.

The patient states that he went to his family doctor who referred him to see me today.

PAST HISTORY

The patient denies any history of multiple sclerosis or brain tumors.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS

The patient reports taking Tylenol for occasional headaches.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Musculoskeletal: Reports right-sided facial pain.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
• Neurological: Follows finger in both directions bilaterally. No sensory loss or numbness in the face on either side.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
• MRI of the head was reviewed today in office and shows small blood vessel abutting and possibly pinching the trigeminal nerve.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
• Trigeminal neuralgia.
• Medical Treatment: Start with gabapentin or Tegretol due to potential side effects associated with Tegretol such as memory loss, tingling, imbalance, dermatologic reactions, particularly Eustachian tube dysfunction.
• Additional Testing: Genetic testing will be ordered to assess for Eustachian tube dysfunction.
• Patient Education and Counseling: Patient will be counseled on potential side effects associated with Tegretol.
• Medical Treatment Initiation: Prescription for gabapentin will be sent over to pharmacy for filling today.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Right knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Michelle King is a 44-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right knee pain. The onset of her symptoms began 1 week ago when she sustained an injury while skiing in Vermont. She was unable to bear weight on her right knee and was taken down by the ski patrol. She reports that she has been experiencing pain on the lateral aspect of her knee, as well as decreased flexion and extension. She denies any numbness or tingling in her toes.

The patient is a very active individual who enjoys skiing and taking care of her 4-year-old twins. She reports that she is currently hobbling around on crutches at home due to her injury. Her husband works a job where he is gone quite a bit, so it is just her and the kids at home.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Reports she is otherwise healthy and denies a history of high blood pressure or diabetes.
Social: Very active with skiing and taking care of her 4-year-old twins. Her husband works a job where he is gone quite a bit.
Medications: Ibuprofen.
Allergies: No known allergies.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

CV: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs.
Respiratory: Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the right knee reveals edema and effusion over the right knee. There is pain to palpation over the right lateral knee joint. Decreased flexion and extension are noted. A positive Lachman sign is present. Palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are present bilaterally. No leg edema in the ankle.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of the right knee obtained today, not yet reviewed.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Right knee pain.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient sustained an injury while skiing in Vermont 1 week ago, which resulted in pain on the lateral aspect of her knee, decreased flexion and extension, as well as a positive Lachman sign on examination. X-ray did not show any bony abnormalities but I am concerned that she has ruptured her ACL or anterior cruciate ligament that helps connect and helps your knee move back and forth so I ordered a MRI just so that we can get a good look at this further confirm that physical exam findings are consistent with this diagnosis.
• Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed treatment options with the patient today including continuing ibuprofen 600-800 mg every 8 hours as needed, wearing a brace for support, and obtaining an MRI for further evaluation.
• Medical Treatment: Continue ibuprofen 600-800 mg every 8 hours as needed for pain management only until MRI results are available.
• Additional Testing: Order MRI of the right knee stat.

Right knee pain.

Rebecca Thompson is a 27-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right knee pain. The onset of her symptoms began 1 month ago when she started swimming more regularly. She has been swimming freestyle with her legs kicking straight out, but she has noticed that her symptoms have worsened after 2 laps. She denies any history of injury.

The patient reports that she has been doing well with her chronic back pain, which has been doing well lately. She denies any lower extremity pain or weakness. The patient reports that she has been doing well with her depression, and that her medication and therapy have been helpful.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right knee pain.
Neurological: Denies lower extremity pain or weakness.
Psychiatric: Reports depression, stable on current medication.
note.objective_exam:

note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of the right knee was reviewed in office today and is normal.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Chondromalacia of the patella.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's x-ray was normal, but she does have patellar inhibition on exam, which is consistent with chondromalacia of the patella.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the nature of her diagnosis and treatment options in detail today. I advised her to avoid activities that put extra pressure on her knees for a couple weeks and to do some straight leg raising exercises to strengthen her quadriceps.
- Medical Treatment: We will start ibuprofen 600 mg four times a day with food today. We will also do some straight leg raising exercises to strengthen her quadriceps.
- Additional Testing: X-ray of the right knee was reviewed in office today and is normal.
2. Chronic back pain.
- Medical Reasoning: Her chronic back pain has been doing well lately, but we will continue to monitor it for any signs of flare up.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the nature of her diagnosis and treatment options in detail today. I advised her to continue swimming as long as it does not cause any increase in symptoms.
- Medical Treatment: Continue as usual.
3. Depression.
- Medical Reasoning: Her depression has been stable on current medication, so we will continue with current medication at this time.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the nature of her diagnosis and treatment options in detail today. I advised her to continue therapy as usual.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Lyme disease.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Michelle Lee is a 31-year-old female with a past medical history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension who presents with abnormal lab findings. She is a positive Lyme titer.

The patient reports that she has been feeling better. She has been feeling tired, really lacking a lot of energy, and she has swollen joints in her elbows, just really hurts. She denies any body aches. The patient was out hiking in the woods and that type of thing a couple of weeks ago, and we thought that that's where she got the bite. She has noticed other rash elsewhere on her body, which she describes as looking like a bull's-eye. The patient denies any high fevers. From a diabetes standpoint, she notes that her blood sugars have been okay but sometimes get a little high and low. She is still taking metformin and lisinopril 10 mg daily.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Endorses fatigue.
• Musculoskeletal: Endorses joint pain.
• Gastrointestinal: Endorses nausea.
• Skin: Endorses rash.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• Constitutional: Normal vital signs.
• Musculoskeletal: Examination of the bilateral elbows reveals swelling bilaterally with pain to palpation.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Lyme titer elevated.
WBC within normal limits.
Other labs normal.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Lyme disease.
- Medical Reasoning: Elevated Lyme titer with symptoms consistent with early disseminated Lyme disease.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the nature of her symptoms and treatment options in detail today.
- Medical Treatment: We will start doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks to treat her Lyme disease. I will also contact an infectious disease specialist to confirm there are no other necessary treatments needed at this time. We will follow up in 1 week for further evaluation.
2. Type 2 diabetes.
- Medical Reasoning: Her hemoglobin A1c was not available at this time but she denies any changes in her blood sugar levels recently.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the nature of her symptoms and treatment options in detail today.
- Medical Treatment: I have ordered an hemoglobin A1c to confirm if any changes are needed to her current medication regimen at this time.
3. Hypertension.
- Medical Reasoning: Her blood pressure is currently within normal limits on examination today, which is consistent with good blood pressure control at home using home blood pressure monitoring devices as well as dietary modifications.

Hannah Phillips is a 52-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of high blood sugar. She reports that she was recently in the emergency room with elevated blood sugar. She denies fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, burning when urinating, joint pain or muscle aches.

She does have a history of osteoarthritis and atrial fibrillation. She reports that her heart races when she is anxious but denies any other symptoms.

She has been doing well with her reflux symptoms and reports that her medication has been helpful.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or shortness of breath.
• Respiratory: Denies cough or dyspnea on exertion.
• Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain or constipation.
• Genitourinary: Denies dysuria or urinary frequency.
• Musculoskeletal: Reports osteoarthritis.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• General Examination: The patient appears in no distress. Her thyroid is slightly enlarged but non-tender. There are no carotid bruits. Her heart rate is irregular and in atrial fibrillation rhythm. Her lungs are clear bilaterally. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender without edema in the lower extremities.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Blood glucose elevated; HbA1c elevated.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Medical Reasoning: Elevated blood glucose and HbA1c levels indicate diabetes mellitus type 2.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed dietary modifications to reduce sugar intake and lifestyle changes to improve overall health status. The patient will receive a glucometer from the nurse for home testing and will be instructed on how to use it.
- Medical Treatment: We started the patient on metformin 500 mg twice daily to help control her blood sugar levels until we receive results from additional labs to determine if she has an autoimmune disorder which would indicate type 1 diabetes mellitus at this time we will hold off on insulin therapy until those results are available.
- Additional Testing: Complete metabolic panel ordered today.
2. Atrial Fibrillation.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's current ECG shows atrial fibrillation rhythm at a rate which is well controlled with metoprolol 25 mg twice daily at this time we will continue her on this medication as prescribed by her current provider.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed lifestyle modifications to reduce anxiety which may contribute to palpitations at home she will follow up with her current provider for further management if needed.
- Medical Treatment: Continue metoprolol 25 mg twice daily as prescribed by current provider.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Yearly follow-up for asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergy.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Emily Hernandez is a 20-year-old female who presents for a yearly follow-up for asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergy. She was last seen in the office in April 2020. Due to insurance changes, she was switched from Symbicort to Wixela. She uses Zyrtec in the spring, summer, and fall for her seasonal allergy symptoms, which tend to work well. She also has known peanut allergy; however, she tolerates almonds and cashews.

The patient reports that her asthma symptoms have been well-controlled with Wixela 250/50 mcg-dose powder for inhalation taken once in the morning and once at night. She states that she rarely uses her albuterol inhaler and only when she is going to be exerting herself. She has been trying to reduce her use of albuterol as she is preparing to join the military soon. The patient reports that she can do things like go on a walk or go to the grocery store without any issues but will take her albuterol before engaging in strenuous activities.

The patient also reports that she has been trying to cut back on vaping and smoking but has been successful in reducing her use of these substances. She states that this may have an effect on her asthma control.

Regarding allergies, the patient reports that she uses Zyrtec more during the spring and fall but not as much during the summer when it is warmer outside. She states that she does not take Zyrtec every day but will take it on days when she knows she will be outside a lot. The patient reports that Zyrtec works well for her seasonal allergy symptoms.

The patient denies any urgent care or ER visits for breathing over the past year.

SOCIAL HISTORY

The patient currently smokes tobacco and vapes; however, she is trying to reduce this use and is interested in cessation in preparation for joining the army.

MEDICAL HISTORY

Medical: Asthma, allergic rhinitis, food allergies to peanut and tree nuts; Montelukast sodium causes a seizure-like reaction.
Allergies: Peanuts cause a severe anaphylactic reaction; Montelukast sodium causes a seizure-like reaction.

The patient reports a history of hypertension.

The patient reports taking Benicar HCT 40 mg/25 mg and Amlodipine 10 mg daily.

Endocrine: Denies polydipsia, polyuria, weight loss, polyphagia.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) with functional abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Brittany Edwards is a pleasant 32-year-old female who presents for a return visit for IBS with functional abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She was last seen in August 2019 with flares of abdominal pain, who was diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome that was treated with Bentyl.

The patient reports that she has been going out to eat on Friday nights and Saturdays and has had some spicy foods or spicy shrimp. She denies that her gut likes it at all. The patient states that she is starting to notice that she is having bowel movements between 2-3 times a day on normal days. Her stools are described as formed. She reports that after drinking alcohol with friends, she tends to have more diarrhea. The patient states that usually they go to Fridays restaurant and she always eats pasta, the chicken alfredo. She normally does not have any issues with this but notes that pasta can make her bloated. Grilled chicken is usually okay but the alfredo sauce is higher in fat and contains dairy. The patient prefers Patron but will only get brown liquor if available. She will occasionally drink a martini.

The patient reports that when she is not eating out or drinking, her daily routine helps keep her regular. When it does flare up, it may not be as bad.

She denies using the fiber supplement Citrucel regularly.

The patient reports that right now she is still having cramping and sharp pains so she has been avoiding heavy foods. She did have some fried chicken today though and everything was alright after that.

She understands the importance of portion sizes so if she eats a little and feels fine then that is okay.

PAST HISTORY

Functional abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; history of flares of abdominal pain; history of poor eating habits; history of poor sleeping habits; history of high stress.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• General Examination: The patient appears stated age. Alert and cooperative in nature.
• Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Brittany Edwards is a pleasant female with IBS and functional abdominal pain aggravated by high stress, poor eating habits, and poor sleeping habits.
• Medical Reasoning: Her symptoms are consistent with IBS which can be exacerbated by dietary triggers such as spicy foods or fatty foods as well as alcohol consumption.
• Patient Education and Counseling: I encouraged dietary modifications such as avoiding greasy or fatty foods as well as sugary drinks when consuming alcohol. We discussed the importance of portion sizes when eating out at restaurants.
• Medical Treatment: We discussed starting a low dose fiber supplement such as Citrucel daily for regularity. If she knows she will be going out to eat at a restaurant where there may be diarrhea, we can start Bentyl 20 mg up to 4 times daily before eating out at the restaurant or repeat the same thing on Saturday if desired. On days when she feels good without symptoms we do not need to use anything else except water for hydration when needed due to nausea.
• Additional Testing: We will try to reduce triggers by watching out for greasy or fatty foods and sugary drinks before taking Zofran if needed.
• Patient Agreements: The patient understands the plan in full and agrees with it.
